summary:
Pará stands under Brazil's national framework. Within that framework the state has its own layer of protection and its own documented gaps: since 2007 a constitutional amendment of the State of Pará has prohibited discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds, and the state's own observances and bodies — Law No. 7261 of 21 April 2009 establishing the State Day to Combat Homophobia, Law No. 10570 of 11 June 2024 establishing the State Day of Bisexual Visibility, and Decree No. 3831 of 8 April 2024 creating the State Council for Sexual Diversity within the State Secretariat for Racial Equality and Human Rights — are framed around sexual orientation rather than gender identity. Gender-identity claims in Pará have therefore been pursued through individual litigation and through the national layer rather than through state statute.

State schools are the clearest area of settled trans-specific provision. Portaria No. 016/2008 of the Pará State Secretariat of Education, issued on 10 April 2008, guarantees travesti and transsexual students in the state public school system the right to use their social name in enrolment, class records, attendance lists and other internal school documents.

Documentation has been contested case by case. On 21 June 2025 Ember Alves Oliveira became the first person in Pará to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker, after the registry office in Ananindeua refused rectification. The registry relied on Provision No. 73 of the National Council of Justice, which does not provide for a third gender option, and refused the first-name change without stating any legal justification, prompting a lawsuit by the Public Defender's Office of the State of Pará. The office argued that documentation failing to reflect a person's gender identity is a source of suffering and anguish and a violation of human dignity.

Access to facilities is the sharpest current exposure. On 14 July 2026 Governor Hana Ghassan signed a law authorising religious temples and schools to restrict bathroom use on the basis of biological sex. Before enactment the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended a veto, arguing that the law would violate the rights of transgender people and the principle of secularism, and on 15 July 2026 the Socialism and Liberty Party announced that it had filed a lawsuit against the measure. A trans visitor entering a temple or a school in Pará now faces a state-authorised restriction that national equality provisions do not automatically displace.

Violence remains documented. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier records 5 trans and travesti people killed in Pará in 2025, out of 80 recorded across Brazil that year. The figure is a raw count from a national tally; no per-capita or population denominator is supplied for Pará, so the number indicates documented killings rather than a comparative risk rate against other states.
tangentialFactors:
Pará's 2025 count of 5 killings comes from a national dossier that ranks Brazil first in world rankings of trans and travesti homicides by raw count. Rankings of that kind track population size and documentation capacity as much as underlying danger, and the sources provide no per-capita basis for placing Pará above or below any other state.

The state's protective machinery and its hostile machinery are advancing simultaneously. The X-marker birth certificate was obtained through litigation in June 2025, while fourteen months later the state authorised sex-based bathroom restrictions in temples and schools over a prosecutor's objection. The bathroom law's challenge was announced on 15 July 2026, one day after signature, so its operative status is unsettled in the available sources.

The state's equality instruments are largely sexual-orientation framed. The constitutional amendment, the two commemorative laws and the State Council for Sexual Diversity address sexual orientation and bisexual visibility; the trans-specific provisions in Pará rest on a 2008 education directive, on case-by-case litigation by the Public Defender's Office, and on the national framework.
localsOnly:
Students in the Pará state public school system may use their social name in enrolment, class records, attendance lists and internal school documents under Portaria No. 016/2008 of the State Secretariat of Education, in force since 10 April 2008.

Residents challenging a registry refusal can proceed through the Public Defender's Office of the State of Pará, which obtained the state's first X-marker birth certificate on 21 June 2025 after the Ananindeua registry invoked Provision No. 73 of the National Council of Justice and refused a name change without stated grounds.

The State Council for Sexual Diversity, created by Decree No. 3831 of 8 April 2024 and seated within the State Secretariat for Racial Equality and Human Rights, is the standing state body for equality matters. Law No. 7261 of 2009 and Law No. 10570 of 2024 designate the State Day to Combat Homophobia and the State Day of Bisexual Visibility respectively.

Since 14 July 2026 religious temples and schools in Pará may restrict bathroom use on the basis of biological sex under state law, a measure the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office had recommended vetoing and which the Socialism and Liberty Party challenged in court on 15 July 2026.
outOfScopeNotes:
Pará's position for 2024 cannot be fixed from the audited sources. The national ANTRA dossier records 122 trans and travesti killings across Brazil in 2024, 16 per cent below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders, but no state-level breakdown for Pará in that year is available here.

No per-capita or population denominator is sourced for Pará, so the 2025 count of 5 cannot be converted into a rate or compared with other states on a like-for-like basis.

The outcome of the Socialism and Liberty Party's challenge to the bathroom law filed on 15 July 2026 is unresolved in the sources, as is whether any suspension has issued in the meantime.

Whether the X-marker precedent set in Ananindeua has been applied by other registry offices across Pará is not sourced, and the reach of the 2025 judgment beyond that single registry is unresolved.
